parts.problem_md: Find the lowest common multiple (LCM) of 40 and 56.
parts.solution_md:
> *Find the prime factors of both numbers 40 and . 56 Factors trees are shown here.*

> * *

![ed-gcse-maths-1-2-pfd-hard-q1-pfds](assets/003-ed-gcse-maths-1-2-pfd-hard-q1-pfds.png)

> *The prime factors of 40 are 2, 2, 2 and 5. *
*The prime factors of 56 are 2, 2, 2 and 7.*

**Correct method ****[1]**

> *The lowest common multiple is the product of the factors which exist in either list, ignoring repeats.   *
*An easy way of finding this is to sort the factors into a Venn diagram and then multiply the factors that are in all sections together.*

> * *

![ed-gcse-maths-1-2-pfd-hard-q1-venn](assets/004-ed-gcse-maths-1-2-pfd-hard-q1-venn.png)

> *Multiply together all of the numbers in the Venn diagram.*

*LCM = 2 × 2 × 2 × 5 × 7*

** ****  LCM = 280 ****[1]**

parts.problem_md:
Buses to Acton leave a bus station every 24 minutes. Buses to Barton leave the same bus station every 20 minutes.

A bus to Acton and a bus to Barton both leave the bus station at 9 00 am.

When will a bus to Acton and a bus to Barton next leave the bus station at the same time?
parts.solution_md:
> *Find the lowest common multiple (LCM) of 20 and 24. List the multiples of both numbers until you find one that is common.*

*20 , 40, 60, 80, 100, 120, 140 ... *

*24, 48, 72, 96, 120... *

**1 mark for each correct list ****[2]**

> *The smallest number that is in both lists is 120. *
*The next time will be after 120 minutes, divide by 60 to find this in hours.*

*120 minutes = 120 ÷ 60 = 2 hours*

> *They will next leave at the same time after 2 hours.*

**11.00 am**** [1]**

parts.problem_md:
`table row cell A space end cell equals cell space 3 to the power of 5 cross times space 5 space cross times space 7 cubed space end cell row cell B space end cell equals cell space 2 cubed cross times space 3 space cross times space 7 to the power of 4 space end cell row cell C space end cell equals cell space 2 to the power of p cross times space 5 to the power of q cross times space 7 to the power of r end cell end table`

Given that

the HCF of $B$ and $C$ is 2<sup>3</sup>× 7 
the LCM of $A$ and $C$ is 2<sup>4</sup>× 3<sup>5</sup>× 5<sup>2</sup>× 7<sup>3</sup>

Find the value of $p,$ the value of $q$ and the value of $r$.

$p=$ .......................................................

$q=$ .......................................................

$r=$ .......................................................
parts.solution_md:
> *We can create a Venn diagram of the prime factors for all three numbers*

> *Only **B** and **C** have a shared factor of 2, and the HCF of **B** and** C** contains the term 2*<sup>*3*</sup>* so this must be in the overlap between **B** and** C** (but not in **A**)*
*As the LCM of **A** and **C** contains 2*<sup>*4*</sup>*, but we know that **A** does not have a factor of 2, the **C** circle (the part which is only **C**) needs an extra 2 to make the total within **C**, 2*<sup>*4*</sup>

![1](assets/012-1.png)

> *Only **A** and **B** have a shared factor of 3, **B** contains 3*<sup>*1*</sup>* and **A** contains 3*<sup>*5*</sup>* so we can put 3*<sup>*1*</sup>* into the overlap between **A** and **B** (but not in **C**), and then 3*<sup>*4*</sup>* into the "only** A**" section*

![2](assets/013-2.png)

*Only **A** and **C** have a shared factor of 5, so there must be a power of 5 in the overlapping region between **A** and **C** (but not in **B**). **A** only contains 5*<sup>*1*</sup>*, so we can place 5*<sup>*1*</sup>* in the overlap* 
*The LCM of **A** and **C** contains 5*<sup>*2*</sup>*, so the remaining 5 must be in the "only **C**" section*

![3](assets/014-3.png)

*All three of **A, B, C** contain a factor of 7, so there must be a power of 7 in the centre* 
*The HCF of **B** and **C** only contains 7*<sup>*1*</sup>*, so the power of 7 in the centre of the diagram will be 7*<sup>*1*</sup>

![4](assets/015-4.png)

*A** contains a factor of 7*<sup>*3*</sup>*, so needs two more 7s* *B** contains a factor of 7*<sup>*4*</sup>*, so needs three more 7s* 
*This means we can put a 7*<sup>*2*</sup>* in the overlap between **A** and **B**, and then the remaining 7 in the "only** B**" section*

![5](assets/016-5.png)

**Correct Venn diagram ****[1]**

> *Now that the Venn diagram is complete, we can read-off the factors of **C*

**C*** = 2×2**<sup>3</sup>**×5×5×7 = 2**<sup>4</sup>**×5**<sup>2</sup>**×7*

> *Recall that** C** was 2*<sup>*p*</sup>*×2*<sup>*q*</sup>*×2*<sup>*r*</sup>

**p**** = 4** 
**q**** = 2**
 **r**** = 1**

**[1]**

**If Venn diagram not used then 1 mark out of 2 for either finding ****r****, or finding ****p**** and ****q**

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

Write 720 as a product of its prime factors. 

Show your working clearly.

Find the smallest whole number that 720 can be multiplied by to give a square number.
parts.solution_md:
> *Method 1*

> *If your answer to (a) is written in the form "2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 × 5" then we can rearrange this to*

*[2 × 2 × 3] × [2 × 2 × 3] × 5*

> *[2 × 2 × 3] × [2 × 2 × 3] is already square so to make the full number square we would need to multiply by another 5 so the number becomes*

*[2 × 2 × 3 × 5] × [2 × 2 × 3 × 5]*

> *Using your calculator to evaluate this number gives*

**3600**** [1]**

> *Method 2*

> *If your answer to (a) is written in the form "2*<sup>*4*</sup>* × 3*<sup>*2*</sup>* × 5" then we can see that "2*<sup>*4*</sup>* × 3*<sup>*2*</sup>*" is already square (all even powers are square numbers, 2*<sup>*4*</sup>* × 3*<sup>*2*</sup>* = [2*<sup>*2*</sup>* × 3] × [2*<sup>*2*</sup>* × 3])*

> *To make the full number square, we would need to multiply by another 5 so the number becomes*

*2**<sup>4</sup>** × 3**<sup>2</sup>** × 5**<sup>2</sup>*

**3600**** [1]**

parts.problem_md:
A machine has a buzzer that sounds every 50 minutes. The machine also has a bell that sounds every 80 minutes.

The buzzer and the bell sound together at 10 am.

Find the time at which they next sound together.
parts.solution_md:
> *We want to find the next time they sound at the same time, this would be after the lowest common multiple of 50 and 80 minutes later*

> *We can list out several multiples of each number, starting with the larger number*

*80, 160, 240, 320, 400, 480, ...*

> *It is easy to spot which would also be a multiple of 50, as multiples of 50 are either 100, 200, 300, ... or 150, 250, etc*

**Listing multiples, or alternatively using a prime factor and venn diagram method ****[1]**

*400 will be the lowest common multiple*

**400 identified ****[1]**

> *So the time they sound together next, will be 10 am plus 400 minutes*

*400 minutes = 400 ÷ 60 hours = 6.66666... hrs* 
*This is 6 hours and 2 thirds, or 6 hours 40 minutes*

*10 am + 6h40m = 16:40*

**16:40** **[1]**

**HCF = 6 ****[2]**

> *Method 2 *

> *Write each number as a product of its prime factors*

$90=2\times3^{2}\times5\,48=2^{4}\times3$

**[1]**

`90 equals bottom enclose bold 2 bold cross times bold 3 end enclose cross times 3 cross times 5
48 equals 2 cross times 2 cross times 2 cross times bottom enclose bold 2 bold cross times bold 3 end enclose`

> *So the highest common factor is *$2\times3$

**HCF = 6 ****[1]**

parts.problem_md:
Martin thinks of two numbers.

He says,

"The Highest Common Factor (HCF) of my two numbers is 6

The Lowest Common Multiple (LCM) of my two numbers is a multiple of 15"

Write down **two** possible numbers that Martin is thinking of.
parts.solution_md:
> *6 is a factor of both numbers so the numbers must both be a multiple of 6. *

> *Choose one of the numbers as 6, to make sure the 6 is the highest common factor (choosing a multiple of 6 could mean that 6 is not the highest common factor).*

> *List the first few multiples of 6.*

*6, 12, 18, 24, 30, 36, ...*

> *  If the lowest common multiple is a multiple of 15, then the lowest common multiple could be 15, 30, 45, 60 etc. *

> *30 is in both lists, so 30 is the second number (a multiple of 6 and 15).*

**Two possible answers are 6 and 30 **** **

**Both numbers have a HCF of 6 ****[1]  **
**Both numbers have an LCM of a multiple of 15 ****[1] **

**There are other possible correct answers, e.g. 12 and 30.**

parts.problem_md: Find the highest **odd** number that is a factor of 60 and a factor of 90.
parts.solution_md:

parts.problem_md:
Here are three lamps.

![q4-1-3-hard-ocr-gcse-maths-extended](assets/031-q4-1-3-hard-ocr-gcse-maths-extended.png)

Lamp **A** flashes every 20 seconds.

Lamp **B** flashes every 45 seconds.

Lamp **C** flashes every 120 seconds.

The three lamps start flashing at the same time.

How many times in one hour will the three lamps flash at the same time?
parts.solution_md:
> *Lamp A flashes every 20 seconds and lamp C flashes every 120 seconds, so lamp C flashes every 6th time that lamp A flashes, as 20 × 6 = 120.*

> *This means you can simply find how many times B and C flash together, as whenever lamp A flashes, C will also be flashing*

> *Find the times when lamps B and C flash together by finding the LCM of 45 and 120. *
*Find the prime factors of both numbers 45 and 120.  *
*Factors trees are shown here.*

![ed-gcse-maths-1-2-pfd-hard-q2-pfds](assets/032-ed-gcse-maths-1-2-pfd-hard-q2-pfds.png)

> *The prime factors of 45 are 3, 3 and 5. *
*The prime factors of 120 are 2, 2, 2, 3 and 5.*

**Correct method ****[1]**

> *The lowest common multiple is the product of the factors which exist in either list, ignoring repeats. *
*An easy way of finding this is to sort the factors into a Venn diagram and then multiply the factors that are in the Venn diagram together.*

![ed-gcse-maths-1-2-pfd-hard-q2-venn](assets/033-ed-gcse-maths-1-2-pfd-hard-q2-venn.png)

> *Multiply together the numbers that are in all sections.*

*LCM  = 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 × 5 = 360*

> *Lamps B and C will flash together every 360 seconds. *

> *Find how many times this is in one hour.*

*1 hour = 60 minutes × 60 seconds = 3600 seconds*

*3600 ÷ 360 = 10 *

**Correct method ****[1]**

** ****  The lamps will all flash together ten times per hour ****[1]**
